result: FLEXIQuant-LF is a label-free computational tool that identifies differentially modified peptides and quantifies modification extent by monitoring unmodified peptide intensities using RANSAC-based robust linear regression, without requiring knowledge of modification types or heavy isotope-labeled reference proteins.
evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C34-C46, C68-C77, C148, and C183-C184 collectively describe the development, implementation, and algorithmic basis of FLEXIQuant-LF. The method is well-documented with clear descriptions of the RANSAC algorithm (C43-C45), normalization procedures (C42), and software implementation (C46). The conceptual foundation building on the original FLEXIQuant method (C35, C69-C72) is logically sound and supported by appropriate citations.

result: FLEXIQuant-LF was applied to DIA/SWATH data of the APC/C complex during nocodazole-induced mitotic arrest in HeLa cells, with 248 out of 289 peptides (86%) meeting quality criteria and showing excellent quantification reproducibility (median Pearson r=0.98).
evaluation: Claims C5, C40, C47-C51, C59-C67, C78-C88, and C174 describe the experimental design and data quality for the proof-of-concept study. The experimental protocol is well-documented with appropriate controls (S-phase as reference), technical replicates, quality control measures (exclusion of 2/12 poor replicates), and high reproducibility metrics. The choice of APC/C is well-justified (C78) with established enrichment protocols and prior characterization.

result: FLEXIQuant-LF successfully identified and quantified modification dynamics in CDC27, classifying 9 peptides as likely differentially modified and 4 as possibly differentially modified, with evidence of modification found for all likely modified peptides and 3/4 possibly modified peptides. The N-terminal region (aa 170-441) showed increasing modification from 36% at 4hr to 65% at 10hr.
evaluation: Claims C89-C99 and C106 demonstrate excellent validation of FLEXIQuant-LF for CDC27. The classification results are well-supported by orthogonal evidence: 5/9 likely modified peptides had phosphorylated cognates identified in DDA data (C94-C95), and all 9 had literature support (C96-C97). The quantification of modification extent (C98-C99) is consistent with prior FLEXIQuant studies (C106), validating the new label-free approach.

result: FLEXIQuant-LF analysis of APC5 identified 4 likely and 5 possibly differentially modified peptides out of 35 quantified peptides, with modification evidence found for all likely modified peptides and 4/5 possibly modified peptides in literature or DDA data.
evaluation: Claims C100-C106 demonstrate successful application to APC5. The classification is well-validated with 2/4 likely modified peptides having phosphorylated cognates in DDA data (C103) and literature support for the remaining peptides (C104). One possibly modified peptide (99LMAEGELK106) lacks literature evidence (C105), which is appropriately acknowledged as either a false positive or novel modification. Results agree with original FLEXIQuant analysis (C106).

result: FLEXIQuant-LF analysis was extended to additional APC/C proteins (APC1, APC4, APC7, APC10, CDC16, CDC20, CDC23), identifying 0-7 likely modified peptides per protein. APC1 showed two distinct regions with different modification kinetics: N-terminal (aa 285-368) reaching 70-71% modification at 10hr versus C-terminal (aa 680-739) reaching 49-64% modification.
evaluation: Claims C111-C123 demonstrate the scalability of FLEXIQuant-LF to multiple proteins. The APC1 analysis is particularly well-supported with 5/7 likely and 3/4 possibly modified peptides having phosphorylated cognates in DDA data (C117), and literature support for an additional peptide (C118). The identification of two regions with distinct modification kinetics (C120-C122) represents a novel biological insight enabled by the peptide-resolved quantification.

result: Reproducibility testing using 1000 runs on 81 MRM samples showed that using 30 RANSAC initiations and selecting the best model resulted in only 44 suboptimal outcomes in 81,000 runs (0.05%), demonstrating very high reproducibility.
evaluation: Claims C52-C53 and C124-C129 describe rigorous reproducibility testing. The methodology is sound: testing on a large independent dataset (81 samples), running 1000 iterations, and systematically evaluating different numbers of RANSAC initiations (C126). The results clearly demonstrate that 30 initiations provide excellent reproducibility (0.05% suboptimal outcomes, C127-C128), justifying the default parameter choice (C129).

result: Validation using in silico modifications on an independent DIA dataset (122 proteins, 1574 runs) showed high correlation between expected and measured changes (Pearson r=0.98), with near-optimal classification performance for likely modified (sensitivity=100%, precision=96.1%) and likely not modified (sensitivity=97.5%, precision=99.1%) peptides, and low quantification errors (mean=0.020, <0.1 for 94.7% of cases).
evaluation: Claims C54-C55 and C130-C139 describe comprehensive validation using ground truth data. The approach is methodologically sound: using an independent public dataset (C54, C130), creating in silico modifications with known change factors (C55, C131-C132), and evaluating both classification and quantification accuracy. The results demonstrate excellent performance with high correlation (r=0.98, C133), high sensitivity/precision for extreme classes (C134), and low quantification errors across different protein sizes (C137-C138).

result: A 'superprotein' approach was developed and validated to analyze proteins with fewer than 5 peptides by combining peptides from multiple proteins with invariable stoichiometry. Application to APC15 and APC16 showed identical classification and near-identical quantification (mean RM score difference=2.45E-10, r²=1) compared to individual protein analysis, revealing no differential modification.
evaluation: Claims C56-C58, C140-C147, C153, and C188-C189 describe the development and validation of the 'superprotein' approach. The rationale is sound: leveraging known equal stoichiometry of APC/C components (C57) while appropriately excluding CDC20 due to changing abundance (C58). The validation is rigorous, showing perfect agreement between individual and superprotein approaches (C145). Results for APC15/APC16 are consistent with literature (C147).

result: FLEXIQuant-LF provides relative modification extent compared to a reference sample rather than absolute quantification. The lower modification extent observed compared to original FLEXIQuant is explained by basal modification levels in the S-phase reference. The current implementation only quantifies increasing modifications, though peptides with decreased modification are reported in output files.
evaluation: Claims C107-C109 and C156-C164 clearly describe important limitations and characteristics of FLEXIQuant-LF. The explanation for lower modification extent (C107-C108) is logical and supported by citation to the original FLEXIQuant study showing 20% basal modification. The limitation to quantifying only increasing modifications (C160-C161) is clearly stated with appropriate workarounds described (C162, C164). The emphasis on relative quantification (C109, C156) appropriately sets expectations.

result: FLEXIQuant-LF requires a minimum of 5 peptides per protein for linear regression, with performance improving with more peptides. The method assumes that the modification state of the majority of peptides does not change, which likely holds for most proteins but may not apply to highly modified proteins like Tau.
evaluation: Claims C149-C152 and C177-C179 describe fundamental requirements and assumptions of the method. The minimum peptide requirement (C151) is justified by linear regression principles (C149-C150), and validation data (C138) confirms robust performance even with 5-7 peptides. The assumption about majority unmodified peptides (C177-C178) is reasonable and appropriately qualified with the Tau exception (C179), demonstrating awareness of method limitations.

result: FLEXIQuant-LF indirectly identifies modified peptides without determining specific modification types or sites. Detailed characterization requires additional analysis or follow-up experiments, but results can guide selection of proteins for synthesis as reference standards.
evaluation: Claims C165-C169 and C190-C191 clearly describe the scope and limitations of FLEXIQuant-LF. The acknowledgment that modification type/site identification is not the objective (C166) is appropriate and honest. The suggestion that results can guide follow-up experiments (C167-C169, C191) is reasonable and demonstrates practical utility despite limitations.

result: FLEXIQuant-LF was applied to a time series experiment but can be applied to case-control studies or cohort comparisons. The 40% modification extent threshold chosen for proof-of-concept is consistent with phosphoproteomics studies, and users can adjust thresholds based on dataset precision with typical specificity-sensitivity trade-offs.
evaluation: Claims C154-C155 and C170-C173 describe the flexibility and parameter choices of FLEXIQuant-LF. The threshold choice (C171) is well-justified by citation to phosphoproteomics literature. The acknowledgment of user-adjustable thresholds (C172) and standard trade-offs (C173) demonstrates appropriate understanding of method characteristics. The broader applicability beyond time series (C155) is a reasonable inference.

result: The combination of affinity purification and DIA analysis facilitated precise and reproducible peptide quantification. DIA is currently the most suitable acquisition method for FLEXIQuant-LF, though the approach is applicable to other label-free quantification methods.
evaluation: Claims C180-C182 describe methodological choices and their rationale. The statement about DIA being most suitable (C181) is supported by the high reproducibility observed (C88) and is appropriately qualified as current best practice while acknowledging broader applicability (C182). The combination of affinity purification and DIA (C180) is well-justified for the proof-of-concept study.

result: Affinity enrichment was used to ensure high peptide coverage for APC/C components. For highly abundant proteins like ribosomes and proteasomes, direct analysis on whole cell lysate may be viable, and future technological developments are expected to enable analysis of less abundant proteins without enrichment.
evaluation: Claims C174-C176 describe the rationale for affinity enrichment and speculate about future applications. C174 is well-supported as a methodological choice for the current study. However, C175 and C176 are speculative (appropriately marked as such in evidence_type) without supporting data. The speculation is reasonable but represents untested hypotheses rather than demonstrated results.

result: FLEXIQuant-LF software is open source and available in GUI and CLI versions via GitHub (https://github.com/SteenOmicsLab/FLEXIQuantLF). Data are available via ProteomeXchange (PXD018411).
evaluation: Claims C6, C81, and C194-C196 describe software and data availability. These are straightforward factual statements about resource accessibility that support reproducibility and are appropriate for a methods paper.

result: FLEXIQuant-LF enables post hoc analysis of any robustly identified protein without heavy isotope-labeled standards, successfully recapitulated modification dynamics from the original FLEXIQuant method, and is expected to enable discovery of novel modification-driven features of health and disease.
evaluation: Claims C185-C187 describe key advantages and validation results that are well-supported by the data presented. C186 demonstrates successful validation against the gold standard original method. However, C192-C193 are speculative about broader impact on the field. While the speculation is reasonable given the demonstrated capabilities, these represent expected rather than demonstrated outcomes.

result: Background context establishes that PTM regulation is non-binary, current MS methods can identify thousands of modified peptides, but quantifying modification extent is crucial. Existing tools (MSFragger, MetaMorpheus, TagGraph) enable PTM identification, while enrichment-based approaches require prior knowledge. The original FLEXIQuant enabled modification quantification but is labor-intensive, and recent isobaric labeling approaches are expensive, highlighting the need for label-free tools.
evaluation: Claims C1-C33 provide background context and motivation for the study. These are well-supported by appropriate citations to prior work (C10-C12, C13, C15, C18-C19, C23, C25-C28, C31) and represent accurate characterization of the field. The logical progression from technological capabilities (C1) through limitations of existing methods (C16-C17, C29-C32) to the need for new tools (C33) effectively motivates the development of FLEXIQuant-LF.
